subject: Career
title: Presenteeism: The Cost of Showing Up Sick
description: A micro-lesson that makes Presenteeism: The Cost of Showing Up Sick usable.

hook.text: She came to work with the flu. Everyone praised her dedication. She infected three coworkers and made 12 errors.

buildup.text: Presenteeism: being physically present but mentally or physically impaired. It costs more than absenteeism.

discovery.text: Harvard estimates presenteeism costs US employers $150 billion annually — far more than sick days.

twist.text: Remote work made presenteeism worse. You can now be 'logged in' with a fever, and nobody even notices.

climax.text: Real productivity requires being genuinely able to work. Taking a sick day isn't weakness — it's efficiency.

punchline.text: Showing up broken costs more than staying home to heal.

quiz.question: How much does presenteeism cost US employers annually?

details.summary: Presenteeism occurs when employees attend work while physically or mentally unwell, resulting in reduced productivity and error-prone output. Studies show presenteeism costs employers more than absenteeism because the hidden productivity loss accumulates unnoticed across entire teams.
details.whyItMatters: Presenteeism costs US employers over $150 billion annually. Understanding this hidden drain helps organizations realize that encouraging rest during illness actually protects overall productivity.
takeaways: Presenteeism reduces productivity by an estimated one-third or more
It costs organizations more than absenteeism combined
Sick employees spread illness, amplifying the productivity loss

faq.question: Why do employees come to work when they know they are unwell?
faq.answer: Drivers include fear of being seen as uncommitted, insufficient sick leave policies, workload pressure with no backup, and cultural norms that glorify toughness. In precarious employment, financial necessity compounds these pressures significantly.

faq.question: How can organizations reduce presenteeism effectively?
faq.answer: Effective strategies include generous paid sick leave, manager training to encourage rest, cross-training so no single person is indispensable, and explicit cultural messaging that staying home when ill protects the whole team.
